title: Where Is the Best Place to Sell Sports Cards? 12 Options Compared
summary: Trading cards are a hot item to sell, but how do you know if your sports memorabilia is worth money? Learn how and where to sell sports cards.

for most sellers, thanks to its large buyer audience, flexible listing formats, and established collectibles market.


However, specialized auction houses, consignment services, and local dealers may be better choices depending on your cards’ value, condition, and how quickly you want to sell.

## The Best Place to Sell Sports Cards for Your Situation


The best way to sell sports cards depends on what you own, how much they’re worth, and your priorities as a seller.


Situation Best Marketplace Why


A graded card worth $100+ Fanatics Collect, ALT, Goldin, or eBay 💎 Specialized auctions attract target collectors; eBay offers broad exposure. Platforms like Fanatics Collect and ALT feature zero seller fee incentive structures on qualifying auctions.


Lowest fees SportsCardsPro or MySlabs ⚡ SportsCardsPro charges no marketplace sales commission; MySlabs charges a flat 3% seller fee plus processing.


Cash Today Local card shop or card show 💵 Sell directly to dealers or collectors in person without waiting for shipping, payout holds, or online buyers.


A box of low-value cards Mercari, COMC, eBay, or Facebook Marketplace 📦 Consign individual cards via COMC, lot them together on Mercari/eBay, or sell bulk lots locally on FBMP to skip individual shipping.

Most Exposure eBay, Whatnot, Mercari, and Facebook Marketplace 🌐 Combining these platforms using a crosslisting tool maximizes total buyer reach while maintaining centralized inventory management.


## The Best Online Platforms to Sell Sports Cards


### **eBay: Best for Reaching the Most Buyers**


eBay is best for reaching the largest audience of sports card buyers, including collectors searching for rare cards and everyday singles.


**Fees:** 13.25% up to $7,500 plus $0.30 or $0.40 per order, or 12.35% for eligible Basic Store subscribers.


**How it works:** Choose fixed-price listings, auctions, or eBay Live. Research sold listings to price cards competitively. Eligible graded cards stored in the PSA Vault can also sell through eBay with one consignment fee.


**Watch out for:** Fees apply to shipping and applicable sales tax, and promoted listings cost extra.


You might also be interested in the article


[eBay Selling Tips: How to Sell on eBay](https://blog.vendoo.co/how-to-get-started-selling-on-ebay)


### **Whatnot: Best for Selling Live**


Whatnot is best for sports card sellers who enjoy live auctions, card breaks, and interacting with collectors.


**Fees:** Sports commissions range from 8% to 6.5%, depending on seller volume, plus 2.9% + $0.30 processing. These tiers began September 21, 2026. A limited-time promotion eliminates commission on the portion of eligible sports singles above $1,500.


**How it works:** Host live shows, run auctions, organize breaks, or create marketplace listings.


**Watch out for:** Live selling requires time and an audience. Processing fees also apply to shipping and taxes.


### **Fanatics Collect (Formerly PWCC): Best for Graded Cards**


Fanatics Collect is best for valuable graded sports cards and collectors seeking specialized auction exposure.


**Fees:** Qualifying graded cards have no seller fee in Weekly and Premier auctions, with potential seller bonuses. Buy Now fees are 6% or 12%, depending on pricing relative to Card Ladder value.


**How it works:** Formerly PWCC, the platform became Fanatics Collect in July 2024. Cards enter its vault before selling through Weekly auctions starting at $5 or Premier auctions targeting items worth $25,000 or more.


**Watch out for:** Buyers pay a 20% premium, and FanCash payouts cannot be withdrawn to a bank account.


### **ALT: Best for Graded Cards With Flexible Selling Options**


ALT is best for graded sports cards, offering fixed-price listings, auctions, and consignment options.


**Fees:** Base-tier fixed-price fees range from 5% to 14%, depending on value. Auctions have no seller fee and offer bonuses of 4% to 15%.


**How it works:** ALT accepts supported PSA, BGS, SGC, and CGC graded cards. It offers free vaulting for qualifying cards worth over $50, Snap to Sell consignment, and auction cash advances of up to 70% for eligible cards valued at $250 or more.


**Watch out for:** Its marketplace focuses on graded cards, and cash advances must be settled against auction proceeds.


### **COMC (Check Out My Cards): Best for Bulk Cards**


COMC is best for sellers with large collections who want to outsource photographing, listing, and shipping.


**Fees:** Standard processing costs $0.65 per raw card or $1.25 per graded card, with a $65 minimum. Fixed-price sales incur a 5% fee, plus 10% when cashing out. Auction fees vary.


**How it works:** Ship cards to COMC, which scans, stores, and lists them. Sellers set prices, and eligible cards can enter eBay auctions.


**Watch out for:** Standard processing takes approximately 16 weeks, and Standard and Select listings have a $100 price cap. Processing and cash-out fees reduce profits.


## Where to Sell Sports Cards Near You: Card Shops and Card Shows


While online selling helps sellers to reach buyers around the world, local selling can provide same-day cash and eliminate the photography and listing process.


Local card shops and sports card shows are the fastest places to sell sports cards for cash, although you’ll generally receive less than you could earn selling directly to collectors online.


Local card shops purchase cards and collections to resell at a profit. Because dealers need room for their own margins, their offers are typically below current market value.


Before visiting, research comparable sold listings and save them on your phone. Get offers from at least two shops, especially when selling valuable cards or an entire collection.


Card shops can also be excellent inventory sources for resellers. Some shops sell inexpensive singles, discounted lots, or collections containing overlooked cards with resale potential.


Sports card shows offer another opportunity to sell directly to collectors and dealers. You can walk the floor and approach dealers with cards for sale or rent a table to sell your own inventory.


If you're bringing cards to a show, organize them by sport, player, or value, and price them beforehand. Consider table rental costs, admission, and travel expenses when calculating your potential profit.


## How to Sell Sports Cards in 6 Steps


Learning how to sell sports cards starts with identifying what you have and understanding what buyers are willing to pay.


1.


**Identify each card** : Find the player’s name, year, manufacturer, set, and card number, usually printed on the back. Don’t forget to look for rookie cards, autographs, limited-edition parallels, and serial-numbered cards.


💡


**Tip:** If you’re unsure what you have, try a reverse image search using Google Lens to find matching cards and identify the exact variation.


2.


**Check the condition:** Inspect corners for wear, edges for chipping, and surfaces for scratches or printing defects. Look for creases, stains, and damage. Check centering by comparing the borders on opposite sides of the card. Even small imperfections can significantly affect a collectible card’s value.


3.


**Research actual selling prices:** Don’t rely on what other sellers are asking. Compare recently sold cards with the same year, set, variation, and condition. Use eBay sold listings, SportsCardsPro, or Card Ladder.


💡


**Tip:** Vendoo’s free eBay Price Checker can help you research comparable sales.


4.


**Decide whether to grade** : Professional grading can increase buyer confidence and resale value, particularly for rare or valuable cards. However, grading is only worthwhile when the potential graded value exceeds the raw value plus grading, shipping, insurance, and other expenses.


💡


**Tip:** Compare recent graded sales before submitting cards to PSA, SGC, BGS, or CGC.


5.


**Choose your selling platform** : Consider the card’s value, condition, selling fees, and how quickly you want to get paid. Use the platform comparison above to identify the best option for your inventory.


6.


**Photograph, list, and ship safely** : Take clear photographs of the front and back in good lighting. Include visible flaws and important card details in your description. Protect cards with a penny sleeve, top loader, and team bag.


💡


**Tip:** For valuable cards, use a sturdy bubble mailer or box with tracking and appropriate insurance.

## The Best Place to Sell Sports Cards Online


The best place to sell sports cards depends on your inventory and selling goals. eBay is the strongest overall option for most cards, while Fanatics Collect, ALT, and other specialized auctions are worth considering for valuable graded collectibles. COMC and local card shops are practical options for selling collections in bulk. ## Selling Sports Cards FAQs


### **Where can I sell sports cards for cash fast?**


Local sports card shops and card shows are the fastest places to sell sports cards for cash. Dealers can evaluate your cards and make offers on the spot, eliminating shipping and waiting for online buyers. However, expect lower offers than individual online sales.


### **How much does eBay charge to sell sports cards?**


eBay generally charges a 13.25% final value fee on sales up to $7,500, plus $0.30 or $0.40 per order. Eligible Basic Store subscribers and higher tiers pay approximately 12.35%. Fees are calculated on the total sale amount, including shipping and applicable taxes.


### **Should I sell my sports cards raw or graded?**


Sell sports cards raw unless professional grading is likely to increase your profit after expenses. Grading is most worthwhile for valuable rookie cards, rare parallels, vintage collectibles, and cards in exceptional condition. Compare raw and graded selling prices, estimate the likely grade, and subtract grading, shipping, insurance, and selling fees before deciding.


### **How do I know what my sports cards are worth?**


Check recently sold listings for cards matching your player’s name, year, manufacturer, set, card number, variation, and condition. eBay sold listings, SportsCardsPro, and Card Ladder provide useful pricing information. Don’t rely on active asking prices, which may be inflated. For graded cards, compare sales with the same grading company and numerical grade.
